front: Which seven common elements exist as diatomic molecules?
back: Hydrogen $\ce{H2}$, nitrogen $\ce{N2}$, oxygen $\ce{O2}$, fluorine $\ce{F2}$, chlorine $\ce{Cl2}$, bromine $\ce{Br2}$ and iodine $\ce{I2}$.
notes: Write them with the 2 in equations, for example chlorine gas is never just Cl.

back: The combining power of an atom or group of atoms. For an ion it is the size of its charge.
notes: $\ce{Al^3+}$ has a valency of 3; $\ce{SO4^2-}$ has a valency of 2.

front: What charges do the ions of Groups I, II, III, VI and VII have?
back: Group I: $1+$; Group II: $2+$; Group III: $3+$; Group VI: $2-$; Group VII: $1-$.

front: Give the formulae of the ammonium, hydroxide, nitrate, carbonate and sulfate ions.
What rule gives the formula of an ionic compound?
back: The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge, using the smallest whole numbers of each ion.
notes: For example $\ce{Al^3+}$ and $\ce{O^2-}$: two Al ($+6$) and three O ($-6$) give $\ce{Al2O3}$.

front: When must a formula contain brackets?
back: When a compound contains more than one of the same compound ion, for example $\ce{Ca(NO3)2}$ or $\ce{(NH4)2SO4}$.
notes: No brackets for a single compound ion: $\ce{Na2SO4}$.

front: What does the (II) in copper(II) sulfate tell you?
back: The copper ion has a $2+$ charge, $\ce{Cu^2+}$, so the formula is $\ce{CuSO4}$.
notes: Roman numerals are used for metals, such as transition metals, that can form ions with different charges.

front: What do the endings **-ide** and **-ate** mean in the name of a compound?
back: -ide: the compound contains just two elements (e.g. sodium chloride). -ate: it contains a compound ion with oxygen (e.g. sulfate, nitrate, carbonate).
notes: Hydroxide is an exception: it ends in -ide but contains oxygen and hydrogen.

back: The number and type of each atom in one molecule of a substance.
The simplest whole-number ratio of the different atoms or ions in a compound.
notes: Ethene $\ce{C2H4}$ has the empirical formula $\ce{CH2}$; the formula of an ionic compound is always an empirical formula.
